title: Where ordering holds, and where it breaks
summary: Kafka orders per partition, RabbitMQ per queue with one consumer; competing consumers, requeues and producer retries reorder, and the cloud brokers have their own ordering keys.

steps.title: Ordering is local, never global
body: No broker gives you a global order across a whole busy topic: that would allow one consumer at a time. What you get is
**order inside a lane**:
```text
Kafka: order per PARTITION                     RabbitMQ: order per QUEUE ... until two consumers share it
P0 | A1:created | A1:paid | A1:shipped |        queue billing: [ A1:created | A1:paid | A1:shipped ]
P1 | B7:created | B7:paid |                              |                    |
(A1 and B7 have no order between them)         consumer c1 gets A1:created (slow: 30 ms)
consumer c2 gets A1:paid    (fast: 5 ms)  -> done FIRST
- **Kafka** keeps records of one partition in order, and one partition has one consumer per group. So "all events of
order A1 in order" means "all events of A1 **on the same partition**", which is what the record **key** gives you.
- **RabbitMQ** delivers a queue's messages in order, but with **competing consumers** they are *processed* in parallel
and finish in any order. A `basic.nack` with `requeue: true` (or a consumer crash) puts a message back while later
messages are already being processed, so it is redelivered **after** them (with `Redelivered = true`).
- For strict per-queue order in RabbitMQ use **one** consumer: `x-single-active-consumer: true` on the queue lets
several consumers stand by while only one receives, with failover. A **stream** (`x-queue-type: stream`) is
RabbitMQ's log with offsets, ordered like a Kafka partition.
> **See it:** in **Labs → Messaging builder → RabbitMQ**, play *Drain the backlog* and watch the completion order with
> two consumers.

steps.prompt: `order-events` has 12 partitions and every record is keyed by `orderId`. What ordering can a consumer rely on?
options: Events of the same order arrive in the order they were written; events of different orders have no defined order
All events arrive in exactly the order they were produced
Events are ordered by timestamp across all partitions
No ordering at all, because there are 12 partitions
explain: The key picks the partition, and a partition is ordered. Two different orders usually sit on different partitions and
are consumed by different members, so their relative order is undefined. Design for "ordered per entity", never

steps.prompt: Two competing consumers with prefetch 1 take messages from one queue. `m1` takes 30 ms, the others 5 ms. Each message goes to the consumer that is free first. In what order do they **finish**?

foreach (var d in done.OrderBy(d => d.At)) Console.Write(d.Msg + " ");

steps.title: Competing consumers: completion order
prompt: Write `List<string> CompletionOrder(string[] messages, int[] durations, int consumers)` that shows what competing
- Messages leave the queue in order; `durations[i]` is how long `messages[i]` takes.
- Prefetch is 1: each message goes to the consumer that becomes free **earliest** (on a tie, the lowest consumer
index); it finishes at that consumer's free time + its duration.
- Return the messages in the order they **finish** (on equal finish times, queue order first).
starter: List<string> CompletionOrder(string[] messages, int[] durations, int consumers)
solution: List<string> CompletionOrder(string[] messages, int[] durations, int consumers)
var done = new List<(long At, int Pos, string Msg)>();
hints: Keep an array `freeAt` with one entry per consumer; pick the index with the smallest value (first one on a tie).
Record `(finishTime, queuePosition, message)` and sort by finish time, then position.
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoMsgs = new[] { "A1:created", "A1:paid", "A1:shipped", "B7:created" };
Dojo.Eq("two consumers: A1:paid finishes before A1:created",
new List<string> { "A1:paid", "A1:shipped", "B7:created", "A1:created" },
CompletionOrder(dojoMsgs, new[] { 30, 5, 5, 5 }, 2));
Dojo.Eq("one consumer keeps the queue order",
new List<string> { "A1:created", "A1:paid", "A1:shipped", "B7:created" },
CompletionOrder(dojoMsgs, new[] { 30, 5, 5, 5 }, 1));
Dojo.Eq("equal finish times keep queue order",
new List<string> { "m0", "m1", "m2", "m3" },
Dojo.Eq("three consumers, one slow message",
new List<string> { "m1", "m2", "m0" },
CompletionOrder(new[] { "m0", "m1", "m2" }, new[] { 5, 1, 1 }, 3));

steps.title: The producer can reorder too: retries in flight
body: A producer keeps several requests **in flight** per broker connection. If batch 1 fails and batch 2 succeeds, the
retry of batch 1 lands **after** batch 2:
```text
in flight:  [seq 0: A1:created]  [seq 1: A1:paid]  [seq 2: A1:shipped]
timeout -> retry      written            written
log:        | A1:paid | A1:shipped | A1:created |          without idempotence
log:        | A1:created | A1:paid | A1:shipped |          with idempotence: seq 1 and 2 are
rejected (OUT_OF_ORDER_SEQUENCE) and resent after seq 0
| Setting | Order on retry | Throughput |
| `enable.idempotence=true`, `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection <= 5` | **kept** (the leader checks sequence numbers) | good |
| idempotence off, `max.in.flight = 1` | kept | poor: one request at a time per broker |
| idempotence off, `max.in.flight > 1` | **can reorder** | good |
The Java client defaults to idempotence on with 5 in flight. **librdkafka defaults `max.in.flight` to 1000000 and
idempotence to off**, so a Confluent.Kafka producer with default settings can reorder records of one key on a retry.
`EnableIdempotence = true` caps in-flight requests at 5 and keeps order.

steps.prompt: Does the order of one entity's messages survive?
items: Kafka, keyed by order id, idempotent producer, one consumer per partition
RabbitMQ queue with three competing consumers
RabbitMQ queue with one consumer that nacks a message with `requeue: true`
RabbitMQ queue with `x-single-active-consumer: true`, handled one at a time
Confluent.Kafka producer with default settings and a retried batch
Service Bus queue with sessions, same `SessionId`
explain: Order survives only when one lane (partition, queue, session, message group) is handled by one consumer at a time,
**and** nothing puts a message back behind later ones (requeue, retry without sequence numbers).

steps.title: Ordering keys in the cloud brokers
body: Every managed broker has the same idea under a different name: **a key that defines the ordered lane**.
| Service | Ordered lane | How you set it | What to know |
| Kafka / Amazon MSK / Confluent Cloud | partition | record key | per partition, one consumer per group |
| Azure Event Hubs | partition | `PartitionKey` | Kafka-compatible endpoint too; consumer groups with checkpoints |

| Azure Service Bus | **session** | `SessionId` on the message, a session-enabled queue or subscription | one receiver holds a session lock at a time; `ServiceBusSessionProcessor` with `MaxConcurrentSessions` processes many sessions in parallel |
| Amazon SQS FIFO | **message group** | `MessageGroupId` | while a message of a group is in flight, the rest of the group waits; `MessageDeduplicationId` dedups within 5 minutes |
| Google Cloud Pub/Sub | **ordering key** | `ordering_key` + message ordering enabled on the subscription | a failed message holds back the rest of its key |
| RabbitMQ | queue | one queue + single active consumer, or a stream | competing consumers give up order |
The shared trade-off is **head-of-line blocking**: one message that keeps failing stops its whole lane, so every one
of these needs a delivery limit (`MaxDeliveryCount`, `maxReceiveCount` in the redrive policy, dead-letter topics,
the quorum queue `delivery-limit`) that moves it aside.

steps.prompt: Match each service to the field that defines its ordered lane.
explain: Same idea everywhere: pick the entity whose events must stay in order (order, account, device) and use its id as the
lane key. Lanes are independent, so many lanes give parallelism and one lane gives order.

steps.title: Retries in flight: with and without idempotence
prompt: Simulate what the leader's log looks like when batches are retried.
Write `List<string> BrokerLog(List<(int Seq, string Value, bool FailsFirst)> batches, int maxInFlight, bool idempotent)`.
Sequence numbers start at 0 and have no gaps.
- The producer works in **rounds**. Each round it sends the first `maxInFlight` pending batches, in sequence order.
- For each batch sent, in order:
- if `FailsFirst` and this is its first attempt, it fails (a timeout) and stays pending;
- else, if `idempotent` and its sequence is not the next one the leader expects, it is rejected
- else the leader appends its value; the next expected sequence becomes `Seq + 1`.
- Pending batches are always kept in sequence order. Repeat until nothing is pending; return the log.
starter: List<string> BrokerLog(List<(int Seq, string Value, bool FailsFirst)> batches, int maxInFlight, bool idempotent)
solution: List<string> BrokerLog(List<(int Seq, string Value, bool FailsFirst)> batches, int maxInFlight, bool idempotent)
var retry = new List<(int Seq, string Value, bool FailsFirst)>();
hints: Loop while anything is pending; each round send the first `Math.Min(maxInFlight, pending.Count)` batches and collect the ones to retry.
`failedOnce.Add(seq)` is true only the first time: use it to fail each `FailsFirst` batch exactly once.
Next round: the retries plus the batches that were not sent, sorted by `Seq` again.
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoB = new List<(int Seq, string Value, bool FailsFirst)> { (0, "A1:created", true), (1, "A1:paid", false), (2, "A1:shipped", false) };
Dojo.Eq("5 in flight, no idempotence: the retry lands last", new List<string> { "A1:paid", "A1:shipped", "A1:created" }, BrokerLog(dojoB, 5, false));
Dojo.Eq("5 in flight, idempotent: order kept", new List<string> { "A1:created", "A1:paid", "A1:shipped" }, BrokerLog(dojoB, 5, true));
Dojo.Eq("1 in flight, no idempotence: order kept (slowly)", new List<string> { "A1:created", "A1:paid", "A1:shipped" }, BrokerLog(dojoB, 1, false));
var dojoTwo = new List<(int Seq, string Value, bool FailsFirst)> { (0, "a", false), (1, "b", true), (2, "c", true), (3, "d", false) };
Dojo.Eq("two failures, no idempotence", new List<string> { "a", "d", "b", "c" }, BrokerLog(dojoTwo, 5, false));
Dojo.Eq("two failures, idempotent", new List<string> { "a", "b", "c", "d" }, BrokerLog(dojoTwo, 5, true));
Dojo.Eq("two in flight, no idempotence", new List<string> { "A1:paid", "A1:created", "A1:shipped" }, BrokerLog(dojoB, 2, false));
Dojo.Eq("nothing to send", new List<string>(), BrokerLog(new List<(int Seq, string Value, bool FailsFirst)>(), 5, true));
